scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The 1715 entry is renamed Saint-Domingue because the mapped west was a French colony, not independent Haiti. Its legacy id, interval and polygon are preserved. Haiti-1815 retains its broad regional identity; the selected-year phase exposes the north-south political division hidden by its imported outline. No successor links are fabricated across the coverage gap.

En Bas Saline’s source gives an approximate opening of 1200 and inconsistent terminal dates of 1520 and 1530. The card uses a contact-era description rather than selecting a false exact abandonment year. Its identification with Guacanagarí’s town and La Navidad remains a proposal, not a proven fact. The town’s chronology does not date the origin or extinction of Taíno people.

Stamps demonstrate patterned cloth, not a recovered shirt. The shirt is explicitly a familiar analogy. Fish-size distributions are observed; identifying mound residents as chiefs is an archaeological interpretation. The material-remains page’s outdated earliest-Caribbean-corn claim is not used.

Puerto Real household evidence is unevenly distributed by status. Imported objects are not proof that all inhabitants enjoyed leisure, literacy or prosperity. Indigenous and African contributions to food preparation are not presented as voluntary participation in colonial labour.

The 1772 regulation is evidence for official restrictions, not a census of dancers or proof of effective enforcement. The forced-labour discussion distinguishes abolition from later coercion and does not identify all post-independence workers as legally enslaved.

UNESCO compresses the transition after Dessalines’s 1806 death; JCB dates the northern presidency and southern republic to 1807. The card describes a period of division beginning after his death, and correctly places the northern monarchy in 1811. It does not make Pétion ruler of the south throughout the entire period or Christophe king from 1806.

The 1906 U.S. diplomatic report supplies only the 1820 and 1822 milestones, checked against the Library of Congress catalogue chronology. Its racial language, assumptions about consent and portrayal of Haitian-Dominican relations are not adopted. The broad 1820 to 1915 phase does not claim unchanged territory, government or all-island rule throughout.

The post-1934 phase is explicitly a broad cultural-history interval, not a political regime. The page does not certify contemporary government, security conditions, hospital availability or programme operation. Modern practices are dated to their source reports.

The soup account describes living heritage and its commemorative role. Frequently repeated claims of a colonial soup prohibition, an exact first independence serving or a named inventor are not adopted without stronger historical evidence. Damas’s family is a specific reported example, not a universal household model.

PIH describes a hospital it helped establish; these are first-party reports, not independent evaluations of clinical effectiveness. The sanitation description does not repeat absolute pathogen-removal claims, national firsts or unsupported contemporary operational assurances.

UNESCO’s living-heritage page and Smithsonian’s Bruno page presented access challenges on direct opening, but their relevant full indexed text was read. AP’s complete indexed report was read; direct access failed. The other cited research pages were read directly.
All new claims were checked by their author and remain pending independent historical review.

proposedOverrides.name: Saint-Domingue
proposedOverrides.summary: French Saint-Domingue occupied western Hispaniola before Haitian independence in 1804. The map’s 1715 to 1783 interval is only a slice of this history.

identityEvidence.assessment: 1715 and 1815 outlines occupy western Hispaniola. The older hispaniola-spain geometry extends east through Puerto Rico and is not associated with this geographic card. Neither near-identical outlines nor a shared narrative establish identical sovereignty or accurate historical borders.

sharedAssociations.basis: Decoded 1715 and 1815 outlines cover the same western Hispaniola region. The card explicitly separates French Saint-Domingue from independent Haiti and the divided states of 1815; see identityEvidence.
